title: How to Politely Decline a Job Offer (or Accept One): Email Templates for Internships and New Grad Jobs
summary: How to politely decline a job offer or accept one: 7 email templates for internships and new grad jobs, plus how to ask for more time or juggle two offers.
body_markdown:
Wondering how to politely decline a job offer without burning the bridge? Respond before the deadline, thank the recruiter, say no in one clear sentence, and keep your reason short. Below are that process and seven copyable emails for declining, accepting, asking for more time and backing out, written for internship and new grad offers.


Summer 2027 offers are landing right now, many with tight deadlines. From the recruiting side, here's what most students don't realize: a fast, polite no is a favor. (It won't feel like one while you're typing it.) The recruiter has a shortlist, and your answer lets them call the next person.


## TL;DR


• Respond before the offer deadline (students usually get about two weeks): call or email the recruiter, thank them, state your decision in one sentence, and keep any reason short.


• Seven copyable templates below cover declining, accepting and asking for more time.


• Before you accept, get the offer in writing and negotiate first, because once you say yes, you stop interviewing everywhere else.


• Two offers, or waiting on a dream company? Ask for time.


• Already accepted and need out? Call the recruiter before you email anyone, and treat backing out as a last resort rather than a plan.

## How Should You Respond to a Job or Internship Offer?


You have three moves: accept, decline or ask for more time. Pick one and tell the recruiter before the deadline, by phone or email, whichever they used to reach you.


Silence is the only wrong answer.


### Accept, Decline or Ask for Time: Your Three Options


**An offer response** is a short written message to the recruiter that says yes, no, or "I need until a specific date," sent before the offer deadline. The format barely changes: thank them, give your decision in one sentence, and confirm next steps.


From the recruitment side: every offer you're sitting on is a seat the company can't give anyone else. Decline quickly and the recruiter reaches their backup while that person is still available.


And save every offer letter. You'll want the dates and titles for your[resume](https://www.extern.com/post/resume-format-types-guide) next season.


### How Long Do You Have to Decide?


**Most students get about two weeks.** According to NACE's 2024 Recruiting Compensation Report, the average number of days students have to respond to a job offer has hovered close to 14 days since 2019 ([NACE, August 2024](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/trends-and-predictions/as-employers-push-out-time-from-interview-to-offer-student-response-time-holds-steady) ).


There's no universal rule. NACE's ethics committee notes that one- to two-week deadlines are common ([NACE advisory opinion](https://www.naceweb.org/career-development/organizational-structure/advisory-opinion-setting-reasonable-deadlines-for-job-offers) ). Schools often set their own floor: Carnegie Mellon gives students until November 15 or three weeks, whichever is later, for offers starting the following year ([CMU offer policy](https://www.cmu.edu/career/employers/hiring-and-offer-policy.html) ). Check your career center's policy before you assume a deadline is final.


## How Do You Politely Decline a Job Offer?


Declining well takes five minutes. The goal: they finish your note and still want to hire you someday.


### 5 Steps to Turn Down an Offer Without Burning the Bridge


1. **Decide for real.** Don't decline as a bargaining move unless you're ready for "okay."


2. **Respond fast.** Once you know it's a no, send it the same day or the next, because waiting a week doesn't make the news any kinder.


3. **Match the channel.** Offer by phone? Call back, then follow up in writing. Offer by email? Email is fine.


4. **Thank them and decline in one sentence.** Name the role and company.


5. **Leave the door open.** Say you'd like to stay in touch, then connect on LinkedIn. A warm decline is networking (see our guide to[getting hired through a DM](https://www.extern.com/post/how-to-get-hired-through-a-dm) ).


### What Reason Should You Give?


You don't owe anyone the full story. One honest, neutral sentence is enough, and the right one depends on why you're saying no.


Why you're declining What to say What to skip


**You accepted another offer** "I've accepted a role that's a closer fit for my goals right now." The other company's name and salary, unless they ask


**The pay is too low** If you'd stay for more, ask before declining. If not: "The compensation doesn't work for me at this stage." Ultimatums and comparisons to friends' offers


**The role isn't a fit** "I've realized the role isn't the right match for what I want to build next." Criticism of the team, the interviews or the work


**Location or remote setup** "I've decided to stay closer to home for now." Long explanations about rent or commutes


**Staying in school** "I've decided to continue my studies this year." Nothing; this one is easy


**Personal reasons** "Due to personal circumstances, I'm not able to accept." Any details you don't want on record


## What Should a Decline Email Say? (Templates)


A good decline email has a clear subject line, a thank-you, a one-sentence decision and a warm close. Copy one below and swap in your details (for email basics, see our guide to[emails employers answer](https://www.extern.com/post/your-ultimate-guide-to-writing-emails-for-employers-that-get-a-response) ).


### Template 1: Declining Because You Accepted Another Offer


**Subject:** \[Your Name\], \[Job Title\] Offer


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thank you so much for offering me the \[Job Title\] position at \[Company\]. I really enjoyed meeting the team and learning about \[specific project or detail\].
>
>
> After a lot of thought, I've decided to accept another offer that's a closer fit for my goals right now, so I'm respectfully declining.
>
>
> I'd love to stay in touch, and I hope our paths cross again.
>
>
> Best, \[Your Name\]


The tone matches a good post-interview note: specific, short, warm. Our[thank-you email guide](https://www.extern.com/post/thank-you-email-after-interview-guide) uses the same formula.


### Template 2: Declining Because the Role Isn't the Right Fit


**Subject:** \[Job Title\] Offer, \[Your Name\]


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thank you for the offer to join \[Company\] as a \[Job Title\], and for the time the team spent with me.
>
>
> I've realized the role isn't the right match for the direction I want to take next, so I'm going to decline.
>
>
> I wish you and the team the best.
>
>
> Sincerely, \[Your Name\]


### Template 3: Declining an Internship Offer (and Keeping Next Summer Open)


Use this if you might want the company later. Finance students coming out of a[superday](https://www.extern.com/post/superday-interview-guide) often hold two bank offers, and today's decline could be next year's full-time target.


**Subject:** Summer \[Year\] \[Internship Title\] Offer, \[Your Name\]


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thank you for offering me the Summer \[Year\] \[Internship Title\] role at \[Company\].
>
>
> I've decided to accept a different internship this summer, so I'm declining with real appreciation. I'm still very interested in \[Company\] and would love to be considered for full-time roles or future programs.
>
>
> Thank you again, \[Your Name\]


### Template 4: Following Up After You Declined by Phone


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thanks for taking my call today. As we discussed, I'm declining the \[Job Title\] offer. I appreciated your help throughout the process and hope we stay in touch.
>
>
> Best, \[Your Name\]


## How Do You Accept a Job or Internship Offer?


Accepting is the fun email, but do your homework first. Once you say yes, you've mostly lost your room to bargain.


### Before You Say Yes: Check These 5 Things


**Get the details in writing before you accept.** A verbal "we'd love to have you" isn't an offer until you see these on paper:


• **Title and team:** the exact role and who you'd report to.


• **Pay:** salary or hourly rate, plus any signing bonus, housing stipend or relocation support that was mentioned on the phone.


• **Start date and location:** on-site, hybrid or remote.


• **Deadline:** the exact date and time they need your answer, including the time zone.


• **Conditions:** background checks, references, work authorization.


If something's off, negotiate now, not after you sign. Our guide on[how to negotiate salary as a new grad](https://www.extern.com/post/how-to-negotiate-salary-as-a-new-grad) has the wording.


But most students aren't juggling a pile of offers. In NACE's 2026 Student Survey, 43% of graduating seniors had at least one job offer before graduation, and the class averaged 0.79 offers each ([NACE, June 2026](https://naceweb.org/about-us/press/2026/more-than-two-out-of-five-of-college-class-of-2026-had-a-job-offer-in-hand-by-graduation) ).


### Templates 5 and 6: Accepting a Job Offer and an Internship Offer by Email


**Template 5: Accepting a full-time job offer**


**Subject:** Offer Acceptance, \[Your Name\], \[Job Title\]


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thank you for the offer! I'm excited to accept the \[Job Title\] position at \[Company\].
>
>
> To confirm, my starting salary will be \[amount\] and my start date is \[date\] at \[location or remote\]. I've signed and attached the offer letter.
>
>
> Please let me know what to complete before my first day.
>
>
> Best, \[Your Name\]


**Template 6: Accepting an internship offer**


**Subject:** Accepting Summer \[Year\] \[Internship Title\] Offer, \[Your Name\]


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> I'm thrilled to accept the Summer \[Year\] \[Internship Title\] offer at \[Company\]. Thank you!
>
>
> I'm confirming my dates of \[start date\] to \[end date\] at \[location\]. Is there anything I should complete before I start?
>
>
> Looking forward to it, \[Your Name\]


Then do the part people forget. Email every company where you're still interviewing and withdraw, politely, the same week.


## What If You Need More Time or Have Two Offers?


Ask early, with a real date. That gets a yes far more often than a vague "can I have more time?"


### How to Ask for an Extension


NACE's ethics guidance tells employers to "be open to reasonable requests for additional time," while warning that an extension may not be granted.


So asking is normal. A yes just isn't guaranteed.


From the recruiting side, three things make an extension easy to approve: a specific date, an honest reason and clear enthusiasm.


**Template 7: Asking for more time**


**Subject:** \[Job Title\] Offer, Timing Question


> Hi \[Recruiter's Name\],
>
>
> Thank you again for the offer. I'm genuinely excited about \[Company\] and the \[Job Title\] role.
>
>
> I'm finishing another interview process and want to make a fully informed decision. Would it be possible to extend my deadline to \[specific date\]? I'll reply sooner if I can.
>
>
> Thanks for understanding, \[Your Name\]


### Waiting on a Dream Company While Holding an Offer


It's common in fall recruiting. NACE's 2025 Recruiting Benchmarks Report found the lag between a first interview and an offer or rejection averaged 27.3 days ([NACE, September 2025](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/trends-and-predictions/employers-make-more-offers-as-student-acceptance-rate-rises-response-time-shortens) ), often longer than your other deadline.


So tell the slower company you have an offer and ask them to speed up. Will they always? No. In our experience, though, plenty of teams can move a final round up a week when they know a candidate might walk. For when consulting firms usually decide, see our[consulting internships summer 2027 guide](https://www.extern.com/post/consulting-internships-summer-2027-guide) .


Your situation Best move


**Offer A's deadline comes before Company B interviews you** Ask A for an extension (Template 7). Tell B you have an offer and ask if they can speed up.


**Company B has you in the final round** Tell B your deadline and ask when they'll decide. Ask A for a few extra days.


**Company B has gone silent** Send one polite follow-up, then decide on A without B.


**You hold both offers** Compare pay, learning, team and location, decide, then decline the other one the same day.


**A return offer vs. a new offer** Ask your current team for honest feedback on growth, and check your school's deadline rules for return offers.


If Company B has gone quiet, our guide on[being ghosted after an interview](https://www.extern.com/post/ghosted-after-interview-2026-summer-internship) has the follow-up to send.


## Can You Back Out of an Offer After Accepting It?


Yes, but it costs something. Backing out after accepting (reneging) is legal in most cases, yet it burns trust with the employer and sometimes your career center.


### What Reneging Costs You


**It's rare, which is why recruiters remember it.** The same NACE compensation report behind the two-week figure found that 75% of offers were accepted, and about 7% of accepted offers later ended with a renege by the candidate.


The employer has already stopped recruiting for your seat, many schools build offer policies around preventing reneges, and recruiters change firms.


But sometimes it's still the right call (a family emergency, a health issue, a clearly better path). Honestly, how you handle it matters more than the decision. Or at least, it's the part you control.


### How to Renege the Least Damaging Way


At Extern, we've seen that the students who keep the relationship are the ones who pick up the phone. The order that works:


1. **Call the recruiter first.** Don't let an email be the first they hear of it.


2. **Apologize once, explain briefly.** "I've had a change in circumstances and can't join as planned. I'm truly sorry for the trouble this causes."


3. **Follow up in writing** the same day with a short version of Template 4.


4. **Return anything they sent** and don't bad-mouth the company.


## What Should You Do Between Accepting and Your Start Date?


Treat the gap as part of the interview. If it's an internship, the summer is your audition for a full-time offer.


### Stay in Touch and Show Up Ready


**Return offers aren't automatic.** NACE's 2025 Internship & Co-op Report found employers extended full-time offers to 62% of their 2024 intern class, the lowest rate in five years ([NACE, August 2025](https://naceweb.org/talent-acquisition/internships/intern-offer-and-conversion-rates-fall-acceptances-rise) ).


So use the months before you start:


• **Send a short check-in** a month or two out.


• **Build the skills the role uses.** Finance offer? Practice modeling. Product offer? Practice writing specs.


• **Plan your return offer now.** Our[intern to full-time offer guide](https://www.extern.com/post/intern-to-fulltime-offer) covers what managers watch for.


An Externship covers the second point. You work on a company-endorsed project with guided support for about 8 weeks at 5 to 10 hours a week, so it fits around classes. In Extern's 2024 outcomes study (July 2024), 75% of participants landed a role within one year of completing.[See which projects are open](https://www.extern.com/externships) .


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is it rude to decline a job offer by email?


No. Email is the normal way to decline, especially if the offer came by email. If the recruiter called you with the offer or you've built a real relationship with them, a quick call first is a nice touch. Follow either one with a short written note so there's a clear record of your decision.


### Do you have to give a reason when you decline a job offer?


No, you don't owe a detailed reason. A short line like "I've accepted a role that's a closer fit for my goals right now" is enough. If pay was the dealbreaker and you'd reconsider at a higher number, say so plainly before you decline. Otherwise, keep it brief and never criticize the company.


### Can declining an offer hurt your chances of working there later?


Not if you decline quickly and politely. Recruiters turn down and get turned down all the time. What sticks is silence, a decline the day before the start date, or reneging without a call. Thank them, keep the note warm, connect on LinkedIn, and you can usually apply again next cycle.


### How soon should you respond to a job offer?


Acknowledge the offer within a day, even if you need time to decide. Thank them and confirm the deadline. Then give your final answer before that deadline, which is usually about two weeks for students. If you already know it's a no, say so right away so they can move to the next candidate.


### Should you accept a job offer over the phone or by email?


Do both. Saying yes on the phone is fine, and recruiters love hearing the excitement. Then send an email or sign the offer letter so the job title, pay and start date are confirmed in writing. Until the written offer is signed, keep the decision tentative and don't resign from anything.
